It’s a voice that’s less grace now than gumption, a ballerina with arthritis hurling herself into the old leaps, trusting the risk to be the reward, trusting the audience to catch her.
Based on this performance, give him his Hamlet already!

Ming-Trent is a high-energy explosion of joy — a striking contrast to the autobiographical material, which begins with his father going to jail when he was a child and includes chapters of homelessness, drug use, and fraught family tension.
What is undeniably real is Ming-Trent’s infectious energy and humor, which he firmly established as a performer.
The actor has an important story to tell, but, in the words of that noted dramaturg, Gertrude, Queen of Elsinore, "More matter with less art."
It’s all a little exhausting, frankly, and indicative of how the performer tries too hard to inject frenetic energy and audience participation into his moving tale.
One of the top one-man shows I've seen this year, full stop.
Whether delivering Shakespeare with hip-hop rhythms, a jazzy beat, or his own syncopations, Ming-Trent is authentic and terrifically entertaining.
How Shakespeare Saved My Life details an absorbing, often haunting journey through the darkness — but offers only fleeting glimpses of the light on the other side.

cn.t: Critics are divided on Ming-Trent's solo show about finding salvation through Shakespeare, with some calling it riveting and moving while others find it more conventional autobiography than transformative testimony. His charismatic performance earns consistent praise.

vr.q: So, I did enjoy the play even though it did not emotionally grab me as much as I wanted it to.
